questions.stem: Deir el-Medina lies in a small desert valley on the west bank at Thebes. Why was the village placed there?
options: It was near the Valley of the Kings, where its men cut the royal tombs
It stood beside the Nile, so its people could farm the richest floodplain
It guarded the main trade route from Thebes to the Red Sea coast
It was next to the temple of Karnak, where its men served as priests
questions.explanation: The village sat in a dry valley within walking distance of the Valley of the Kings and the Valley of the Queens. Its people did not farm; the state supplied their food and water.

questions.stem: Deir el-Medina had no well or nearby river. How did the village get its water?
options: Water carriers brought it up from the cultivation, often using donkeys
A canal from the Nile ran directly to a reservoir inside the village wall
Rainwater collected on the flat roofs supplied most of the year's needs
Each house had a deep well dug through the rock to reach groundwater
questions.explanation: Support staff, including water carriers, delivered water to the village, and records note donkeys used for the job. Thebes has almost no rain, and there was no canal to the site.

questions.stem: The workers of Deir el-Medina worshipped which royal pair as the patrons and founders of their village?
options: Thutmose III and his wife Merytre-Hatshepsut
Ramesses II and his queen Nefertari
Akhenaten and his queen Nefertiti
Amenhotep I and his mother Ahmose-Nefertari
questions.explanation: Amenhotep I and Ahmose-Nefertari were deified and worshipped in the village for centuries. Nefertari of Ramesses II's reign is a different queen.

questions.stem: The village's patrons were Amenhotep I and Ahmose-Nefertari, yet the earliest bricks from its enclosure wall are stamped with the name of Thutmose I. What is the best conclusion?
options: The bricks prove that Amenhotep I and Thutmose I were the same king under two names
The cult of Amenhotep I began only after the village was finally abandoned
Thutmose I destroyed an earlier village that Amenhotep I had built on the site
The walled village may date from Thutmose I, with its patrons honoured later
questions.explanation: Many scholars think the walled village dates from Thutmose I, while Amenhotep I and his mother, who may have begun the royal tomb workforce, became its divine patrons. The evidence shows the cult and the buildings are not the same thing.

questions.stem: Near the end of the 20th Dynasty, the workmen left Deir el-Medina and moved inside the walls of Medinet Habu. Why?
options: Raids and unrest on the west bank made an unwalled valley unsafe
A flood of the Nile destroyed the houses and filled the village with silt
The king ordered all tomb building to move north to the Delta
The village was burned down after the workers' strike in Year 29
questions.explanation: In a time of Libyan raids, weak royal authority and insecurity, the workmen moved within the fortified temple of Ramesses III at Medinet Habu. The strike happened decades earlier and the village was not destroyed after it.

questions.stem: Which Egyptologist found the intact tomb of the architect Kha and his wife Meryt in 1906?
options: Mariette
Schiaparelli
Bruyere
Maspero
questions.explanation: The Italian Egyptologist Schiaparelli found the tomb, and its contents went to the Egyptian Museum in Turin. Bruyere led the French excavation of the village later, from the 1920s.

questions.stem: Bernard Bruyere led excavations at Deir el-Medina for about three decades from the 1920s. What was his main contribution?
options: He removed the best tomb paintings and sold them to museums in Europe
He deciphered hieratic script for the first time using the village's ostraca
He found the village by chance while searching for the tomb of Amenhotep I
He cleared and recorded the village, its houses and its cemeteries
questions.explanation: Working for the French Institute in Cairo, Bruyere excavated and recorded the village, the cemeteries and a great pit full of ostraca. The village was known long before his work, and hieratic had already been read.

questions.stem: Jaroslav Cerny is best known in the study of Deir el-Medina for:
options: conserving the painted burial chamber of Sennedjem after floods damaged it
using aerial photography to map the paths between the village and the valley
publishing the village's ostraca and papyri to rebuild its community
digging the first trenches through the village using hired workers in the 1880s
questions.explanation: Cerny, a Czech Egyptologist, spent decades on the village's written sources, identifying workmen, families and crews. His study of the Ramesside workmen's community is a key work.

questions.stem: The tomb of Sennedjem was found intact in 1886 and opened under Gaston Maspero, head of the Antiquities Service. Why is this tomb important?
options: It is the only royal tomb ever discovered inside the village of Deir el-Medina
Its walls record the full text of the workers' strike under Ramesses III
It held the mummies of all the kings whom the villagers had buried
Its painted burial chamber and goods show a workman's own burial in fine detail
questions.explanation: Sennedjem, a servant in the Place of Truth under Seti I and Ramesses II, decorated his own vaulted burial chamber. It shows what skilled workmen could do for themselves.

questions.stem: Nineteenth-century work at Deir el-Medina, such as Auguste Mariette's, differed from later excavation. Which limitation of early work most affects historians today?
options: Early excavators photographed everything, but the glass negatives were too dark
Early excavators refused to dig in the village because it was not royal
Early excavators recorded too much detail for anyone to publish it
Finds were often taken without recording where in the site they came from
questions.explanation: Early clearances often aimed at objects for museums, so many ostraca and papyri lost their context, and some were scattered in collections. Later excavators such as Bruyere recorded findspots and layers.

questions.stem: A historian says Deir el-Medina gives 'a typical picture of ordinary life in Egypt'. Which is the strongest objection?
options: Its records were all written by kings, so they show no ordinary people
Almost no written sources survive from the village, only its buildings
It was a Greek settlement, so its customs were not Egyptian at all
Its literate, state-paid craftsmen were unlike most farmers
questions.explanation: The village's skilled, often literate workmen were paid by the state and lived in a closed community, so it is unusually well documented but not typical. Peasant farmers left little writing.

questions.stem: Thousands of ostraca were recovered from a great pit north of Deir el-Medina. Why did so many texts end up there?
options: The pit was used as a dump, so discarded notes, letters and records piled up
The pit was a sealed royal archive where scribes stored the state's papyri
Robbers hid the texts there to stop them being used in their trials
The villagers buried their texts there as offerings to the goddess Meretseger
questions.explanation: The pit became a rubbish dump, and limestone flakes and potsherds with writing on them were thrown in. Ostraca were cheap scrap, unlike papyrus, which is why so many survive.

questions.stem: Besides the crew of tomb builders, the village relied on support staff called the smdet. Their jobs included:
options: carrying water, cutting wood, fishing and washing clothes
carving the tomb walls and painting the scenes in the burial chambers
keeping the accounts of the crew and writing the daily work journal
serving as soldiers in the army of the king on campaign in Nubia
questions.explanation: The support staff lived outside the walled village and supplied water, fish, wood, vegetables and laundry. The scribe of the tomb kept the records, and the crew did the carving and painting.

questions.stem: The workmen did not work every day. Which pattern do the records show?
options: A seven-day week, with one day off for the worship of Amun each week
Work only during the flood season, when farmers had nothing else to do
Work every day of the year except during the king's own funeral
A ten-day week, usually with two days off, plus festivals
questions.explanation: The Egyptian week was ten days long, and the crew usually rested at its end and on festivals. During the working days they often slept in huts near the work site rather than returning home.

questions.stem: A register from the reign of Ramesses II lists why men missed work, including 'brewing beer', a scorpion sting and embalming a relative. What does it best show?
options: Workers were punished severely for every day missed, whatever the reason
Most workers were too sick to work for most of the year in this period
The crew worked only when the king himself visited the Valley of the Kings
Absences were recorded, and family reasons were accepted
questions.explanation: The scribe noted each man's absences and reasons, which included illness, family duties and religious obligations. The register shows organised record keeping, not harsh punishment.

questions.stem: Ostraca show workmen making coffins, statues and furniture for private clients in their spare time. What does this suggest about the village economy?
options: Skilled men could add to their rations through private work
The state banned all private work, so these ostraca must be forgeries
Workmen earned nothing from the state and relied entirely on private work
Only the scribe was allowed to trade, since he could write the contracts
questions.explanation: The crew received grain and other goods from the state, but they also sold their skills privately, recording prices and exchanges. This side business helped some families become prosperous.

questions.stem: On monuments and in texts at Deir el-Medina, a married woman is often given the title nebet per, which means:
options: God's Wife of Amun
great royal wife
wise woman
lady of the house
questions.explanation: Nebet per, 'lady of the house', describes a married woman running a household. God's Wife of Amun and Great Royal Wife were titles of royal women.

questions.stem: Ostraca record villagers consulting a 'wise woman' (ta rekhet) when misfortune struck, such as the death of a child. What role did she play?
options: She acted as the judge of the village court and sentenced criminals
She was the chief priestess who ran the temple of Hathor in the village
She trained the girls of the village to read and write hieratic
She advised on which god or spirit had caused the trouble
questions.explanation: The wise woman was consulted about the divine or spirit causes of illness and death. The village court, the kenbet, was made up of local men such as foremen and scribes.

questions.stem: Which is the main limitation of the written record for women at Deir el-Medina?
options: Texts about women were all destroyed in the robberies of the 20th Dynasty
Women wrote most of the texts, so they exaggerate their own importance
Most texts were written by men, so women appear through men's concerns
Women are never mentioned, so nothing is known about them at all
questions.explanation: Literacy was mostly male, so women appear in men's letters, accounts, wills and court records. They are mentioned often, owning property and going to court, but rarely in their own words.

questions.stem: Village houses were long and narrow. Which feature is typical of the front room?
options: A stone pool collecting rainwater through an opening in the roof
A courtyard garden with fruit trees and a fishpond in the centre
A shrine to the Aten with an open altar for offerings to the sun
A raised brick platform whose purpose historians debate
questions.explanation: Many front rooms held a raised platform, the lit clos, often painted with Bes or women. Historians have suggested a household shrine, a place linked to childbirth or a bed. The rainwater pool describes a Roman atrium.

questions.stem: In the second room of many houses, families kept small stone busts and stelae of an 'excellent spirit of Re'. These show that villagers:
options: honoured dead relatives at home and sought their help
worshipped the king as the only god in the village
kept portraits of the foremen to show their loyalty
believed the dead could not affect the living in any way
questions.explanation: Ancestor busts and akh iqer en Ra stelae were the focus of offerings to deceased family members, who were thought able to help or harm the living. This was a domestic cult, not worship of the king.

questions.stem: Meretseger, worshipped by the villagers, was a cobra goddess linked with:
options: the peak above the royal tombs, called 'she who loves silence'
the Delta marshes, and called the protector of the infant Horus
the Nile flood, and usually shown as a pregnant hippopotamus
the city of Memphis, and shown as a fierce lioness of war
questions.explanation: Meretseger was the goddess of the Theban peak above the royal tombs. The pregnant hippopotamus describes Taweret, a household goddess also popular in the village.

questions.stem: The deified Amenhotep I gave oracles at Deir el-Medina. How did this work?
options: Questions were written on bones, which were heated until they cracked
His statue was carried, and its movements were read as answers
A priest went into a trance and spoke in the dead king's voice
The king's mummy was opened each year so that its signs could be read
questions.explanation: Bearers carried the statue, and its movement towards or away from a person or written question was taken as the god's decision, even in property disputes. Cracked bones describe Shang divination.

questions.stem: The burial chamber of Thutmose III's tomb in the Valley of the Kings is notable because:
options: it was cut into the floor of the temple of Karnak to keep it near Amun
it is the largest tomb in the valley, with over a hundred chambers
it was left plain because the king died before it could be decorated
it is oval like a cartouche, with the Amduat painted like a papyrus
questions.explanation: The chamber's rounded shape recalls a cartouche, and the Amduat is painted in simple outline figures on a pale background, like a papyrus scroll. The tomb with over a hundred chambers is KV5, for sons of Ramesses II.

questions.stem: How did the crew decorate the walls of a royal tomb?
options: Sculptors carved freehand without any plan, since the king approved each scene later
Scenes were painted on papyrus in workshops and then glued to the walls of the tomb
Draughtsmen drew outlines in red on plaster, and sculptors and painters followed
Painters worked first, and then the plasterers covered the paint with a protective layer
questions.explanation: Draughtsmen sketched scenes in red, corrected them in black, and sculptors and painters worked from these outlines. Unfinished tombs show every stage.

questions.stem: The scribe of the tomb recorded the copper chisels issued to each man and weighed them when they were returned. Why?
options: Copper was valuable, so weighing stopped workers keeping metal
The weight showed how many hours each man had worked in the tomb
Heavier chisels were given to foremen to show their higher rank
The king paid the crew by the weight of stone they had removed
questions.explanation: Copper was costly state property, so tools were issued and checked by weight to detect loss or theft. Records of lamp wicks used were also kept.

questions.stem: Workmen built their own tombs on the hillside beside the village. What was distinctive about many of them?
options: A huge stone pyramid like those built for Old Kingdom kings at Giza
A temple on the east bank of the Nile where priests made daily offerings
A plain pit in the sand with no decoration, chapel or tomb goods
A small mud-brick pyramid above an offering chapel
questions.explanation: Many workmen's tombs had a chapel topped by a small pyramid, with painted burial chambers cut below. Skilled men used their training on their own tombs.

questions.stem: The tomb of Kha and Meryt contained linen, food, furniture, Meryt's cosmetic box and a measuring rod given to Kha. What makes this find so valuable?
options: It proves that every family in the village was buried with great wealth
Its walls are covered in the longest painted scenes in any Theban tomb
It contained the royal mummies moved there for safety by priests
Its intact goods show the burial of a non-royal official
questions.explanation: Because it was found intact, the tomb shows a full set of possessions of an 18th Dynasty overseer of works and his wife. Kha was well off, so it cannot speak for every family.

questions.stem: The painted burial chamber of Sennedjem shows him and his wife ploughing and harvesting in lush fields. This scene represents:
options: the Field of Reeds, the ideal afterlife where the dead farmed
the estates Sennedjem was given by the king as a reward for his work
the land of Punt, reached by Hatshepsut's trading expedition
the village of Deir el-Medina as it looked in Sennedjem's lifetime
questions.explanation: The Field of Reeds (Iaru) was an idealised afterlife landscape of abundant crops. The workmen were not farmers in life, which shows the scene is religious rather than a record of daily life.

questions.stem: Papyrus Salt 124 records accusations by the workman Amennakht against the foreman Paneb. Which charges did it include?
options: Selling the plans of the royal tombs to Libyan raiders from the west
Forging the king's seal to obtain extra rations of grain for himself
Theft from a royal tomb, violence and misconduct with women
Leading the strike in Year 29 and marching on the temple of Karnak
questions.explanation: Amennakht accused Paneb of many crimes, including stealing from the tomb of Seti II, assault and adultery. The text is one-sided, as the accuser also had his own grievance over the foremanship.

questions.stem: In Year 16 of Ramesses IX, Paser, the mayor of the east bank of Thebes, made accusations about tomb robbery. Who did he clash with?
options: Pawero, the mayor of the west bank, who oversaw the necropolis
Paneb, the foreman accused in Papyrus Salt 124 under the 19th Dynasty
Ramesses IX himself, who had ordered the royal tombs to be emptied
Herihor, the high priest of Amun, who later took royal titles at Thebes
questions.explanation: Paser reported robberies on the west bank, which Pawero controlled, and the inspection recorded in the Abbott Papyrus followed. The rivalry between the two officials shapes how the evidence was reported.

questions.stem: In the Leopold-Amherst Papyrus, a stonemason confesses to robbing the tomb of a king and his queen, stripping the gold and burning the coffins. Why must a historian use this confession with care?
options: It was written centuries later by Greek writers who had never visited Thebes
It is a work of fiction from a scribal school that copied famous stories
It was invented by Howard Carter to explain the state of the royal tombs
It was given at a trial where suspects were beaten in questioning
questions.explanation: The robbery trials record that suspects were beaten during questioning, so details may have been shaped by pressure. Even so, the papyri give rare evidence of how tomb robbery worked.

questions.stem: Which explanation best links the strike of Year 29 with the later wave of tomb robberies?
options: The tombs were robbed by foreign soldiers who replaced the striking workmen
Late payments and weak royal control left workers poor and tombs poorly guarded
The strikers robbed the tombs on the day of the strike to protest against the king
Robberies stopped completely after the strike, because the workers were paid more
questions.explanation: Supply problems under Ramesses III and the declining authority of later kings led to hardship and lax control of the necropolis, conditions in which robbery spread. Several thieves came from local workers and officials.
